rows.ideal_execution_standard: Keep the head up and eyes locked entirely on the target through the entirety of the strike to protect the neck.
Immediately open the hips by pivoting strictly 90 degrees toward the play-side perimeter.
Extend both arms down and out, utilizing a smooth, two-handed underhand scooping motion.
Flick the wrists dynamically upon release to create a natural, end-over-end tumble.
rows.fault_trigger: "Spinning the Ball". Trying to throw a spiral on a toss, which makes the ball highly unstable in the air and incredibly difficult for a moving running back to track and catch cleanly.

rows.ideal_execution_standard: Place the pitch precisely 1 yard out in front of the running back's numbers so they can catch it in full stride.
Keep the chest pointing forward to actively threaten the defense as a runner, with the ball tucked securely with two hands near the chest.
Attack the outside shoulder of the unblocked read-key edge defender to force them to commit.
Hold the attack trajectory until the defender physically commits to your chest.
rows.fault_trigger: Staring Down the Target. Looking directly at the pitch man or shovel receiver early, alerting the linebackers and allowing them to jump the play.

rows.ideal_execution_standard: Extend the arms and deliver a crisp, one-handed thumb-down flick (Speed Option) or a soft, two-handed basketball chest pass (Interior Shovel).
The arms pump hard at chest height in a genuine sprint-start rhythm, matching what a real slant release would look like.
rows.fault_trigger: Passive or low-amplitude arm action that does not match a real sprint, leaving the upper body out of step with the feet and weakening the fake.

rows.ideal_execution_standard: The drive leg holds an acute bend - roughly 110 to 130 degrees - producing maximum ground force to launch onto the diagonal.
rows.fault_trigger: Drive leg too straight at push-off, producing little ground force, so the attack step lacks the urgency needed to make the fake believable.

rows.ideal_execution_standard: The shoulders rotate fully square to the 45 degree line with the torso driving low and forward, exactly as they would on a genuine slant.
rows.fault_trigger: Shoulders lagging behind the feet or staying upright rather than driving low onto the diagonal, so the upper body never commits to the lie.

rows.ideal_execution_standard: The hips accelerate along the 45 degree path and rotate fully onto the inside diagonal, committing the whole body to the fake from the first step.
rows.fault_trigger: Hips staying square while only the feet take the diagonal, so the fake is not sold and a disciplined defender reads the outside release immediately.

rows.ideal_execution_standard: The head locks straight down the 45 degree inside path from the first step, selling the route rather than checking on the defender.
rows.fault_trigger: LOOKING AT THE DEFENDER - peeking at the DB instead of locking down the 45 degree track, which breaks the illusion before it is established. (Gaze itself is not pose-measurable - orientation only.)

rows.ideal_execution_standard: The back foot fires outward on a sharp 45 degree diagonal toward the inside lane, launching straight onto the diagonal track with no ground given up first.
rows.fault_trigger: SOFT FIRST STEP - taking a tentative, short step instead of an aggressive 45 degree launch. The tight end must look like he is sprinting a slant from step one. Also: losing ground backward before the step fires.

rows.ideal_execution_standard: The torso stays low and forward in an aggressive sprinting posture through the push step, matching what a genuine slant would look like.
rows.fault_trigger: Torso rising toward upright during the push step, which tips that a plant is coming rather than a continued sprint inside.

rows.ideal_execution_standard: The hips stay dropped and fully committed to the inside trajectory, holding the low sprinting position that makes the fake believable.
rows.fault_trigger: Hips rising through the push step, so the tight end looks like he is preparing to stop rather than sprinting a route - the defender reads the cut coming.

rows.ideal_execution_standard: The back knee drives high and hard on the push step, simulating full sprint acceleration so nothing about the movement suggests a fake.
rows.fault_trigger: Low knee drive on the push step, betraying that the tight end is not truly accelerating and is already preparing to plant.

rows.ideal_execution_standard: The head stays locked straight down the inside path through the push step, holding the deception right up until the plant.
rows.fault_trigger: Head turning back toward the outside before the plant, breaking the deception early and letting the defender sit on the breakout. (Gaze itself is not pose-measurable - orientation only.)

rows.ideal_execution_standard: The arm pump continues at full amplitude through the push step, sustaining the impression of a slant or post being run at full effort.
rows.fault_trigger: Arm pump dropping off during the push step, which signals to the defender that the tight end is about to stop rather than continuing inside.

rows.ideal_execution_standard: The opposite foot drives down the exact same 45 degree line as the first step, taking real ground inside so the fake reads as a committed route.
rows.fault_trigger: The second step drifting off the 45 degree line or shortening, so the diagonal track bends and the defender reads that the inside move is not real.

rows.ideal_execution_standard: On the third step the outside foot slams into the turf along the 45 degree line and grips, acting as a violent brake that kills the inside momentum in one contact.
rows.fault_trigger: The plant foot sliding or drifting at contact rather than gripping, so the momentum is not arrested and the tight end needs extra steps to change direction.

rows.ideal_execution_standard: The head holds the inside fake alignment right up to the exact plant frame, then prepares to snap back - the deception is maintained to the last possible instant.
rows.fault_trigger: Head starting to turn back outside before the plant lands, giving the defender an early warning and letting them jump the breakout. (Gaze itself is not pose-measurable - orientation only.)

rows.ideal_execution_standard: The outside hand crosses over the chest frame at the plant, shielding the body against any late contact from a defender closing on the fake.
rows.fault_trigger: Hands staying wide or low at the plant, leaving the chest unprotected at the exact moment a defender who bought the fake is arriving. (Finger and grip detail needs the Hand landmarker.)

rows.ideal_execution_standard: The planting knee flexes deep - roughly 90 to 110 degrees - creating a spring-loaded platform to drive back out toward the sideline.
rows.fault_trigger: Planting on a stiff, straight leg, which cannot absorb the momentum or store energy - the tight end slides through the cut and the breakout has no power.

rows.ideal_execution_standard: The hips drop sharply and shift slightly back at the plant, sinking to absorb the forward momentum and load the push back outside.
rows.fault_trigger: POP-UP BRAKING - letting the chest and hips rise when trying to stop. Without sinking the hips to absorb the momentum, the tight end slides or stumbles instead of cutting cleanly.

rows.ideal_execution_standard: The shoulders stay over the toes as the plant foot lands, keeping the body stacked over the brake and ready to snap back toward the outside.
rows.fault_trigger: Chest rising or the shoulders falling behind the plant foot, so the weight sits back and the tight end cannot push cleanly back to the outside.

rows.ideal_execution_standard: The trailing arm executes a heavy downward chop past the shoulder line, clearing the defender's arms as the tight end breaks back to the outside.
rows.fault_trigger: No hand action at the breakout, or an arm path that never crosses the shoulder line, leaving a recovering defender's hands attached through the escape. (Specific hand technique needs the Hand landmarker.)

rows.ideal_execution_standard: The outside knee drives high toward the sideline and upfield, taking immediate ground and building instant separation out of the cut.
rows.fault_trigger: Low knee drive out of the breakout, so the first strides are short and the tight end takes too long to convert the cut into separation.

rows.ideal_execution_standard: The inside shoulder rolls away from the defender as the tight end breaks out, turning the chest off them and eliminating the jersey surface they could grab.
rows.fault_trigger: LEAVING THE CHEST EXPOSED - turning back outside with the chest wide open, which invites a trailing defender to land a heavy recovery punch and push the tight end off his path.

rows.ideal_execution_standard: The plant foot drives explosively back toward the outside, the step reversing direction sharply enough to complete the diamond path and escape into the open lane.
rows.fault_trigger: A rounded or gradual change of direction rather than a sharp reversal, so the diamond flattens into a curve and the defender recovers the ground the fake bought.

rows.ideal_execution_standard: The hips snap violently open toward the sideline, flipping the body off the inside track and onto the outside release in one decisive rotation.
rows.fault_trigger: Hips opening slowly or only partway, so the tight end drifts out of the cut rather than exploding, and the separation the fake created is given straight back.

rows.ideal_execution_standard: The head snaps round toward the sideline and upfield the instant the breakout fires, re-establishing vision to locate the quarterback and track the football.
rows.fault_trigger: Head coming round slowly after the breakout, so the tight end is late finding the quarterback and the ball on a route designed to come out quickly. (Gaze and ball location are not pose-measurable.)

rows.ideal_execution_standard: The head stays level and locked forward toward the defender's belt line - reading the hips rather than the hands or the feet.
rows.fault_trigger: Head dipping toward the feet or lifting off the defender's midsection line during the kickstep. (Gaze itself is not pose-measurable, and the defender is not in frame - orientation only.)

rows.ideal_execution_standard: The front knee holds an acute bend - roughly 100 to 120 degrees - absorbing force and storing elastic energy for the escape rather than straightening under the load.
rows.fault_trigger: Front knee straightening or losing its bend during the kickstep, so no energy is stored and the escape has to be generated from a standing start.

rows.ideal_execution_standard: The torso holds a slight forward lean over the toes while the shoulders stay square to the defender, giving away nothing about the intended release direction.
rows.fault_trigger: Shoulders rotating open during the kickstep and telegraphing the release, or the torso leaning back away from the defender instead of staying over the toes.

rows.ideal_execution_standard: Hips stay sunk low through the kickstep, holding the loaded height established in the stance with no upward rise.
rows.fault_trigger: Hips rising during the kickstep, unloading the legs and costing the elastic energy needed to escape.

rows.ideal_execution_standard: Hands stay active and up around lower chest height, ready to fight the defender's hands, never dropping below the hips.
rows.fault_trigger: Hands dropping below the hips during the kickstep, leaving the tight end unable to counter the jam. (Finger and grip detail needs the Hand landmarker.)

rows.ideal_execution_standard: The rear foot kicks directly behind the front foot to load the release, without giving up ground backward. The step loads the body rather than retreating from the line.
rows.fault_trigger: Stepping backward and losing ground to the defender, or kicking the rear foot wide of the front foot rather than directly behind it, which widens the base and slows the escape.

rows.ideal_execution_standard: The front foot plants firmly with no braking, and the feet stay tight within the body's frame - at or inside shoulder width - so the escape can fire in either direction.
rows.fault_trigger: Planting with a braking action that kills momentum, or a base widening beyond shoulder width so the tight end has to gather before escaping.

rows.ideal_execution_standard: The shoulders stay tucked inside the width of the knees, keeping the frame compact so the defender cannot read which way the release is going.
rows.fault_trigger: A shoulder drifting outside the knee line at the plant, widening the frame and telegraphing the release direction before the crossover begins.

rows.ideal_execution_standard: The hands retract tight to the lower chest and ribcage in a compact ready position, loaded to swipe or punch as the escape begins.
rows.fault_trigger: Hands hanging away from the frame or extended early, giving the defender something to grab and leaving nothing loaded for the escape. (Finger and grip detail needs the Hand landmarker.)

rows.ideal_execution_standard: Both knees bend deeper at the plant, dropping the tight end into a loaded crouch that can launch in any direction.
rows.fault_trigger: Knees staying at their kickstep angle or straightening at the plant, so the tight end is upright and committed rather than loaded and able to go either way.

rows.ideal_execution_standard: The hips drop and shift slightly back over the plant foot, compressing like a spring so the escape can launch in any direction.
rows.fault_trigger: Hips staying high or drifting forward past the plant foot, so the spring never loads and the escape has no power behind it.

rows.ideal_execution_standard: The head stays level through the plant, holding a neutral forward line rather than dropping to look at the feet as the body loads.
rows.fault_trigger: Head dipping toward the feet as the body loads at the plant, losing sight of the defender at the moment the release is about to start. (Gaze itself is not pose-measurable - orientation only.)

rows.ideal_execution_standard: The lead knee flexes and drives aggressively inward across the body, pointing along the inside fake path to sell the release direction.
rows.fault_trigger: Lead knee staying square or trailing the foot across, so the lower body does not commit and the fake reads as a feint rather than a release.

rows.ideal_execution_standard: The arms pump hard toward the inside lane in time with the crossover step, mimicking a genuine release so the fake is complete from feet to hands.
rows.fault_trigger: Arms staying passive during the crossover, or pumping late so the upper body lags the feet and the fake looks manufactured. (Finger and grip detail needs the Hand landmarker.)

rows.ideal_execution_standard: The push off the plant foot drives the rear foot sharply across the body's midline into the inside lane, committing hard enough to sell the inside release.
rows.fault_trigger: A lazy crossover that never clears the midline, or one too slow to be believed - the defender does not bite and the outside lane never opens.

rows.ideal_execution_standard: The inside shoulder dips hard and the torso leans into the inside lane, committing the upper body to the fake so the defender has to honour it.
rows.fault_trigger: Shoulders staying level through the crossover, so the upper body never sells the inside move and the defender stays square to the outside release.

rows.ideal_execution_standard: The hips drive hard laterally across the defender's face, rotating toward the inside lane so the whole body sells the fake rather than just the feet.
rows.fault_trigger: Hips staying square while only the feet cross over - the fake is not sold, and the defender reads the outside release immediately.

rows.ideal_execution_standard: The head snaps sharply toward the inside lane in time with the crossover, adding the final piece of the fake - the defender reads the eyes as well as the feet.
rows.fault_trigger: Head staying still or turning too slowly during the crossover, leaving the fake incomplete. (Gaze itself is not pose-measurable - orientation only.)

rows.ideal_execution_standard: The inside shoulder rolls away from the defender - getting skinny - so the tight end presents the narrowest possible surface as he clears the contact window.
rows.fault_trigger: Running through the release square-shouldered, presenting a full chest for the defender to get hands on and re-route the tight end.

rows.ideal_execution_standard: The head snaps back upfield to align with the route, re-establishing vision quickly so the tight end can track the cushion and find the ball.
rows.fault_trigger: Head staying turned toward the fake after the escape, or turning back slowly, so the tight end loses track of the defender and is late finding the ball. (Gaze and ball location are not pose-measurable.)

rows.ideal_execution_standard: The crossover foot plants and immediately pushes off into the outside lane - no gather step, no pause. The redirect is instantaneous, converting the fake straight into the escape.
rows.fault_trigger: A gather step or hesitation between the crossover and the burst, giving the defender time to recover and closing the outside lane the fake just opened.

rows.ideal_execution_standard: The trailing arm drives sharply past the shoulder plane - swipe, chop or swim - clearing the defender's hands as the body escapes outside.
rows.fault_trigger: No hand action at the escape, or an arm path that never clears the shoulder plane, leaving the defender's hands attached through the release. (Specific hand technique needs the Hand landmarker.)

rows.ideal_execution_standard: The hips rotate sharply from the inside fake toward the sideline and upfield, converting the lateral momentum of the crossover into vertical drive up the field.
rows.fault_trigger: Hips rotating slowly or incompletely, so the tight end drifts sideways out of the release instead of driving upfield, losing ground on the route stem.

rows.ideal_execution_standard: The outside knee drives high and the trailing leg extends fully at push-off, taking ground upfield immediately rather than shuffling out of the release.
rows.fault_trigger: Low knee drive and an incomplete trailing-leg extension, so the first strides out of the release are short and the tight end takes too long to reach full speed.

rows.ideal_execution_standard: Both knees hold a consistent bend - roughly 120 to 140 degrees - through the slide, producing a smooth lateral glide with no upward bounce.
rows.fault_trigger: Knees extending during the slide, which pops the body upward into a hop; or collapsing so deep the tight end cannot cover ground laterally.

rows.ideal_execution_standard: The shoulders stay wide, level and square to the defender, moving with the hips rather than rotating independently of them.
rows.fault_trigger: Shoulders rotating away from the hips during the slide, disconnecting the upper body and signalling the release direction before the tight end has committed.

rows.ideal_execution_standard: The hips travel horizontally at a constant height with no rotation, staying square to the defender so the slide gives away nothing about the eventual release.
rows.fault_trigger: Hips rotating during the slide, opening the tight end to the defender and tipping the release; or the hips rising and falling, which turns a glide into a hop.

rows.ideal_execution_standard: The head stays level and locked on the defender's belt line throughout the slide, tracking them laterally without dropping to the feet.
rows.fault_trigger: Head dropping to watch the feet during the slide, or turning upfield early and telegraphing the vertical release. (Gaze itself is not pose-measurable - orientation only.)

rows.ideal_execution_standard: The hands stay up at lower chest height and relaxed through the slide, ready to react the instant a jam comes.
rows.fault_trigger: Hands dropping as the tight end concentrates on the footwork, leaving him with no answer if the defender reaches out mid-slide. (Finger and grip detail needs the Hand landmarker.)

rows.ideal_execution_standard: The tight end pushes off the front foot and slides the back foot sideways, feet staying wide and parallel and low to the ground, moving laterally to bypass the jam rather than through it.
rows.fault_trigger: THE BUNNY HOP - jumping or leaping sideways instead of sliding. Hopping lifts both feet too high off the ground, leaving the tight end completely vulnerable if a defender jams him mid-air. Also: feet crossing rather than staying parallel.

rows.ideal_execution_standard: Both knees stay deep and stable through the pause, absorbing the lateral momentum and holding balance on the wide base.
rows.fault_trigger: Knees straightening or wobbling during the hesitation, so the tight end loses balance on the wide base or unloads the legs before the transition.

rows.ideal_execution_standard: The hips stay low and loaded through the hesitation, holding the compressed position so the forward transition can fire without a reset.
rows.fault_trigger: Hips rising during the pause, unloading the spring - the tight end then has to sink again before transitioning, which gives the defender time to recover.

rows.ideal_execution_standard: The hands retract tight to the lower ribcage into a compact ready position, loaded to strike as soon as contact comes.
rows.fault_trigger: Hands hanging loose or away from the frame during the pause, giving the defender something to grab and leaving nothing loaded for the strike. (Finger and grip detail needs the Hand landmarker.)

rows.ideal_execution_standard: The head stays locked forward on the defender through the pause, reading whether their hips open or freeze before the tight end commits to the vertical.
rows.fault_trigger: Head turning upfield during the hesitation, tipping the vertical release before the read is complete. (Gaze and the defender's reaction are not pose-measurable.)

rows.ideal_execution_standard: The torso tilts slightly forward over the toes to threaten an immediate vertical launch from the side lane, while the shoulders stay quiet and give nothing away.
rows.fault_trigger: LEANING EARLY - tilting the head or shoulders toward the intended vertical route during the micro-pause, which completely tips off the true direction. Also: leaning back rather than forward, so no vertical threat is presented.

rows.ideal_execution_standard: The sliding foot plants firmly and the lateral movement stops dead for a fraction of a second, holding the wide base while the defender is frozen.
rows.fault_trigger: Drifting through the hesitation rather than stopping cleanly, so there is no freeze for the defender to react to and the bait never lands.

rows.ideal_execution_standard: The outside foot slams aggressively into the turf and grips, arresting all lateral momentum in one contact so it can be converted straight into forward drive.
rows.fault_trigger: SOFT CLEAT PLANT - failing to slam the outside foot into the turf with force. A soft plant results in a slow, sluggish transition from horizontal to vertical, and the foot drifts rather than gripping.

rows.ideal_execution_standard: The head begins turning upfield toward the release lane as the plant lands, leading the body into the vertical transition.
rows.fault_trigger: Head turning well before the plant (telegraphing the vertical) or lagging behind it, so the body commits before the tight end has picked up the lane. (Gaze itself is not pose-measurable - orientation only.)

rows.ideal_execution_standard: The planting knee bends sharply - roughly 90 to 110 degrees - absorbing the lateral energy of the slide and converting it into straight-line power.
rows.fault_trigger: Planting on a stiff, straight leg, which cannot absorb the lateral force - the tight end slides through the plant or has to take a recovery step before going vertical.

rows.ideal_execution_standard: The inside shoulder dips at the plant, lowering the chest profile and getting skinny against the defender's leverage as the transition begins.
rows.fault_trigger: Staying square and upright through the plant, presenting a full chest just as the tight end commits and giving the defender a clean target to re-route.

rows.ideal_execution_standard: The hands come up fast into an aggressive strike position as the plant lands, ready to meet the defender if they reach out at the transition.
rows.fault_trigger: Hands staying passive or low through the plant, leaving the tight end defenceless at the exact moment the defender is most likely to reach. (Specific hand technique needs the Hand landmarker.)

rows.ideal_execution_standard: The hips sink further at the plant, loading the lower body so the lateral energy can be redirected into forward acceleration.
rows.fault_trigger: Hips staying level or rising at the plant instead of sinking, so nothing loads and the transition to vertical has no power behind it.

rows.ideal_execution_standard: The trailing arm drives violently past the shoulder plane - swipe, chop or club-rip - shattering the defender's reach as the tight end clears vertically.
rows.fault_trigger: DROPPING THE HANDS - letting the arms trail behind the body, leaving no protection against a recovering defender's arm bar or jersey pull. Also: an arm path that never clears the shoulder plane. (Specific hand technique needs the Hand landmarker.)

rows.ideal_execution_standard: The inside shoulder rolls away as the tight end bursts past, turning the chest off the defender and eliminating the jersey surface they could grab.
rows.fault_trigger: Bursting through square-shouldered, leaving a full jersey surface exposed for a recovering defender to grab as the tight end passes.

rows.ideal_execution_standard: The plant foot drives explosively forward, accelerating the tight end past the defender's hip plane and clearing their level in one burst rather than easing into the route.
rows.fault_trigger: A slow or gradual push-off out of the plant, so the tight end never clears the defender's level and stays inside their reach as the route develops. (Defender position is not in frame - path and acceleration only.)

rows.ideal_execution_standard: The hips flip sharply from the lateral slide orientation to point straight upfield, locking the tight end onto the vertical track in a single decisive rotation.
rows.fault_trigger: Hips rotating slowly or only partway, leaving the tight end running at an angle across the field rather than vertically - the slide's advantage is lost in the transition.

rows.ideal_execution_standard: The lead knee drives high out of the transition, taking immediate ground upfield and accelerating the tight end toward top speed.
rows.fault_trigger: Low knee drive out of the burst, so the first strides are short and shuffling and the tight end takes too long to reach full speed after the transition.

rows.ideal_execution_standard: The head comes fully round to track upfield along the route, re-establishing vision quickly so the tight end can process cushion and locate the ball.
rows.fault_trigger: Head still turned toward the slide side after the burst, or coming round slowly, so the tight end is late reading coverage and late finding the ball. (Gaze and ball location are not pose-measurable.)

rows.ideal_execution_standard: The hands come up quickly to chest height into a tight, relaxed ready position as the feet land - loaded to strike but not tense.
rows.fault_trigger: Hands staying low or arriving late, so the tight end has nothing ready when the defender's hands come. (Finger and grip detail needs the Hand landmarker.)

rows.ideal_execution_standard: Both feet leave the ground at the same instant, the back foot snapping forward and the front foot back, landing parallel and wider than shoulder width to establish a balanced, uncommitted base.
rows.fault_trigger: OVER-SPLITTING - landing far too wide, which locks up the hips so the tight end cannot push off to change direction. Also: feet leaving the ground at different times rather than together, or landing staggered instead of parallel.

rows.ideal_execution_standard: Both knees bend deep into an athletic squat - roughly 90 to 110 degrees - with weight balanced evenly over the balls of the feet, ready to drive in any direction.
rows.fault_trigger: Knees staying too straight to load the split, or weight settling back onto the heels so the tight end cannot push off cleanly.

rows.ideal_execution_standard: The head stays level and locked on the defender's belt line through the split, with no downward dip toward the feet as the body resets.
rows.fault_trigger: Head dropping to watch the feet during the split, losing sight of the defender at the moment the read has to happen. (Gaze itself is not pose-measurable - orientation only.)

rows.ideal_execution_standard: The hips drop the instant the feet land, lowering the centre of gravity immediately so the base is established and loaded in a single motion.
rows.fault_trigger: Landing tall and sinking afterwards, so there is a moment where the tight end is upright and unloaded - the split buys no advantage if the hips arrive late.

rows.ideal_execution_standard: The shoulders stay perfectly square to the defender through the split, with the torso leaning slightly forward over the knees to shield the chest.
rows.fault_trigger: Shoulders rotating during the split, which tips the release direction before the tight end has even read the defender.

rows.ideal_execution_standard: The hips stay low through the read, preserving the loaded position so the tight end can explode in whichever direction the defender opens.
rows.fault_trigger: Hips rising during the hesitation, unloading the base - the tight end then has to re-sink before moving, which costs the advantage the split created.

rows.ideal_execution_standard: Quiet shoulders - no tilt, no rotation, no lean. The upper body gives away nothing while the tight end reads which way the defender is going.
rows.fault_trigger: LEANING EARLY - tilting the head or shoulders toward the intended release during the micro-pause, which completely tips off the true direction and wastes the freeze.

rows.ideal_execution_standard: Both knees hold their deep flexion through the read - loaded springs, ready to extend the instant the defender commits.
rows.fault_trigger: Knees straightening during the hesitation, so the springs unload and the drive-off has to start from scratch.

rows.ideal_execution_standard: The head stays locked on the defender's midsection through the read, processing whether they freeze, lean, or slide before the tight end commits.
rows.fault_trigger: RUSHING THE READ - turning the head toward the intended path before the defender has declared, or skipping the read entirely and committing blind. (Gaze and the defender's reaction are not pose-measurable.)

rows.ideal_execution_standard: The hands stay up at chest level and active through the read, ready to strike the moment the defender's hands come.
rows.fault_trigger: Hands dropping or going passive during the hesitation, leaving the tight end with nothing ready when the jam arrives. (Finger and grip detail needs the Hand landmarker.)

rows.ideal_execution_standard: The feet stay planted wide and parallel through the read - completely still, holding the base while the defender is frozen.
rows.fault_trigger: Feet shuffling, creeping or resetting during the read, which breaks the freeze and tells the defender a move is coming.

rows.ideal_execution_standard: The hips turn and open violently toward the chosen lane the instant the plant foot hits, converting the loaded base into directional drive.
rows.fault_trigger: Hips opening slowly or lagging behind the plant, so the drive has no rotational force behind it and the tight end pushes sideways instead of exploding through the lane.

rows.ideal_execution_standard: The leading shoulder dips into the direction of the release - getting skinny - so the tight end presents the smallest possible target as he attacks the lane.
rows.fault_trigger: Driving into the lane square-shouldered and upright, presenting a full chest for the defender to get hands on and re-route the release.

rows.ideal_execution_standard: The foot opposite the intended path slams cleanly into the turf with no slide, delivering full force to drive the body laterally and forward into the open lane.
rows.fault_trigger: CLICK-BACK - dragging the driving foot instead of slamming it cleanly into the turf, which bleeds away the explosive power. Also: the foot sliding at contact rather than gripping.

rows.ideal_execution_standard: The hands fire up and forward as the plant lands - striking, clearing or bypassing the defender's jam in the same instant the body drives.
rows.fault_trigger: Hands staying passive through the drive, leaving the defender free to land a clean jam on a tight end who is already committed to a direction. (Specific hand technique needs the Hand landmarker.)

rows.ideal_execution_standard: The drive leg extends fully to deliver every bit of force, while the lead knee flexes and drives forward to take immediate ground into the lane.
rows.fault_trigger: Drive leg failing to extend fully, leaving force in the ground; or the lead knee not driving through, so the first stride out of the plant is short.

rows.ideal_execution_standard: The head snaps toward the chosen attack path as the plant fires, committing the whole body to the direction in one motion.
rows.fault_trigger: Head turning before the plant (telegraphing the direction) or well after it (leaving the tight end driving blind into the lane). (Gaze itself is not pose-measurable - orientation only.)

rows.ideal_execution_standard: The hips rotate fully to point straight downfield, locking the tight end onto the vertical track so the route can develop at full speed.
rows.fault_trigger: Hips never finishing their rotation, leaving the tight end running at an angle across the field rather than vertically, which costs separation and distorts the route.

rows.ideal_execution_standard: The trailing arm drives sharply past the shoulder plane with a swift chop, clearing the defender's frame as the tight end locks onto the vertical track.
rows.fault_trigger: DROPPING THE HANDS - letting the arms trail behind the body, leaving no protection against a recovering defender's arm bar or jersey pull. (Specific hand technique needs the Hand landmarker.)

rows.ideal_execution_standard: The escape step drives straight upfield on a tight angled path past the defender's hip, clearing their level entirely rather than drifting wide or running into them.
rows.fault_trigger: SLAMMING INTO THE DB - releasing directly into the defender's body instead of taking an angled, tight path past their hip. The aim is to clear their frame, not initiate a collision. Also: drifting wide of the track and losing ground. (Defender position is not in frame - path tightness only.)

rows.ideal_execution_standard: The head comes round to track straight upfield, re-establishing vision quickly so the tight end can read coverage depth and locate the football.
rows.fault_trigger: Head staying turned toward the release side after the escape, or coming round slowly, so the tight end is late reading coverage and late finding the ball. (Gaze and ball location are not pose-measurable.)

rows.ideal_execution_standard: The trailing shoulder rolls inward and away as the tight end clears, eliminating the jersey surface a recovering defender could grab.
rows.fault_trigger: Escaping square-shouldered, leaving a full jersey surface exposed for a trailing defender to grab or arm-bar.

rows.ideal_execution_standard: The outside knee drives high through the escape strides, building linear speed immediately and creating separation from the defender.
rows.fault_trigger: Low knee drive out of the escape, so the first strides are short and shuffling and the tight end takes too long to reach full speed.

rows.ideal_execution_standard: The front knee lifts high through the swing phase on every stride, sustaining genuine top-end speed down the stem.
rows.fault_trigger: Knee lift dropping off during the stem, which slows the tight end and signals that he is preparing to break rather than running deep.

rows.ideal_execution_standard: The head stays locked straight downfield through the stem, selling the vertical route and giving the defender nothing to read.
rows.fault_trigger: Head turning toward the break direction during the stem, tipping the route before the tight end has reached the break point. (Gaze itself is not pose-measurable - orientation only.)

rows.ideal_execution_standard: The hips carry constant high-speed forward travel with minimal vertical bounce - all the energy goes into covering ground down the stem.
rows.fault_trigger: Velocity dropping off during the stem, or excessive vertical bounce wasting energy - either way the deep threat is not sold and the defender does not have to respect it.

rows.ideal_execution_standard: The arms pump at full amplitude past the ribcage throughout the stem, driving the sprint and giving no indication a break is coming.
rows.fault_trigger: Arm pump shortening or slowing during the stem, an early visual tell that the tight end is about to break.

rows.ideal_execution_standard: The torso holds an aggressive forward lean over the toes through the stem, matching what a genuine deep sprint looks like.
rows.fault_trigger: Torso rising toward upright during the stem, which reads as a tight end preparing to stop rather than one running past the defender.

rows.ideal_execution_standard: Stride length stays maximal and constant through the vertical stem - the tight end runs at genuine top speed so the deep route is believable right up to the break.
rows.fault_trigger: STUTTER STEPPING - stride length shortening or step frequency rising before the break point, which tells the defender a cut is coming and surrenders the advantage the stem was built to create.

rows.ideal_execution_standard: The shoulders stay completely square to the stem and forward over the knees during the load - the upper body reveals nothing while the lower body prepares.
rows.fault_trigger: Shoulders starting to rotate toward the break during the load step, an early tell that lets the defender jump the route.

rows.ideal_execution_standard: The hips drop a small, controlled amount to load the cut - without losing any forward speed. The sink is subtle enough that the defender cannot see it coming.
rows.fault_trigger: POPPING UP - a sudden upward spike in hip or chest height, destroying the low sprint angle and broadcasting the break. Also: sinking so far that forward velocity drops and the cut becomes a gather.

rows.ideal_execution_standard: The arm pump continues exactly as it was through the stem - unchanged amplitude and rhythm, so nothing about the upper body signals the load.
rows.fault_trigger: Arm mechanics changing during the load step - shortening, tightening or breaking rhythm - which gives the defender a visual cue that the break is imminent.

rows.ideal_execution_standard: Stride length holds at its full stem value through the load step while the weight quietly prepares to transfer laterally - nothing shortens or gathers.
rows.fault_trigger: Stride shortening on the load step, which is a visible gather and tells the defender the break is one step away.

rows.ideal_execution_standard: The lead knee bends more deeply on the load step, absorbing the downward force of the sink while keeping the tight end stable at full speed.
rows.fault_trigger: Lead knee staying stiff through the load step, so the sink cannot be absorbed and the tight end either pops up or loses balance going into the plant.

rows.ideal_execution_standard: Vision stays fixed downfield right through the load step, holding the deep threat until the exact frame the transition begins.
rows.fault_trigger: Head beginning to turn during the load step rather than at the transition, breaking the deception one step too early. (Gaze itself is not pose-measurable - orientation only.)

rows.ideal_execution_standard: The shoulders turn in time with the head, tilting into the new direction so the upper body initiates the cut and blindsides the defender before the feet move.
rows.fault_trigger: Shoulders lagging behind the head turn or staying square, so the upper body does not lead the cut and the transition has to be driven entirely by the plant.

rows.ideal_execution_standard: Both knees stay actively bent through the bait, loaded and ready to handle the high-speed lateral shift that the plant is about to demand.
rows.fault_trigger: Knees extending during the bait, so the tight end arrives at the plant unloaded and cannot absorb the lateral force - the cut slips or rounds.

rows.ideal_execution_standard: The feet keep tracking straight under the body along the stem while the upper body begins to turn - the lower body has not yet committed to the break.
rows.fault_trigger: Feet drifting off the stem line during the bait, so the lower body commits before the plant and the cut loses its sharpness.

rows.ideal_execution_standard: The hips begin to uncoil toward the break direction, starting the rotation that the plant will complete.
rows.fault_trigger: Hips rotating fully before the plant, committing early and letting the defender break on the route; or not uncoiling at all, so the plant has to do all the work and the cut rounds off.

rows.ideal_execution_standard: The arms pull in tight to the body as the turn begins, tightening the frame so the tight end can rotate faster into the break.
rows.fault_trigger: Arms staying wide through the bait, slowing the rotation and costing the tight end time in the break. (Finger and grip detail needs the Hand landmarker.)

rows.ideal_execution_standard: The head snaps hard and fast toward the new route trajectory, leading the whole movement - the eyes get there first and the body follows.
rows.fault_trigger: BLIND TURNING - head yaw lagging behind the hip and shoulder rotation, meaning the tight end is turning blind rather than leading with his eyes, and will be late seeing the ball. (Gaze itself is not pose-measurable - orientation only.)

rows.ideal_execution_standard: The torso tilts sharply inward toward the new route angle at the plant, countering the centrifugal force of the cut and keeping the tight end balanced through the turn.
rows.fault_trigger: Staying upright through the plant, so momentum carries the tight end wide and the cut rounds off; or over-leaning and losing balance out of the break.

rows.ideal_execution_standard: The plant knee drops into deep flexion at contact, loading the leg as a high-speed spring that will fire the tight end out on the new line.
rows.fault_trigger: Planting on a stiff leg, which cannot absorb the speed or store energy - the tight end either slides through the cut or has to take recovery steps before accelerating.

rows.ideal_execution_standard: The outside cutting foot lands with the toe already pointed along the new route path, steering the body into the break rather than braking against it. The toe is pulled up into dorsiflexion so the heel bites the grass first, giving clean, firm contact instead of a slide or a stubbed toe. The step stays compact and lands directly beneath the centre of mass - no over-extending or lunging - which preserves body control and keeps the defender believing the tight end is still running vertically until the instant the weight drops.
rows.fault_trigger: THE BLIND PLANT - the foot lands still pointing straight downfield instead of along the new path, so the tight end slides outward, loses his base, and the cut becomes a skid rather than a redirect. Toe left down (plantarflexed) rather than pulled up, so the tight end slides through the plant or stubs the toe instead of biting the ground heel-first. Over-extending or lunging the plant step out ahead of the centre of mass, which costs body control and tips the break early.

rows.ideal_execution_standard: The hips snap open to exactly the angle the head and the plant foot have already established - head, foot and hips all pointing down the same new route line.
rows.fault_trigger: Hips opening to a different angle than the head and plant foot, so the body fights itself through the cut and the exit line is wrong.

rows.ideal_execution_standard: The arms stay tucked tight to the chest through the plant, keeping the frame compact so the body rotates as fast as possible into the new direction.
rows.fault_trigger: Arms flying wide at the plant, slowing the rotation and costing time in the break - and often unbalancing the tight end as he exits. (Finger and grip detail needs the Hand landmarker.)

rows.ideal_execution_standard: By the plant the head is fully locked down the new route corridor, already looking for open space and the football before the body has finished turning.
rows.fault_trigger: Head still rotating at the plant rather than already locked on the new corridor, so the tight end comes out of the cut late to find the ball. (Gaze and ball location are not pose-measurable.)

rows.ideal_execution_standard: The inside foot drives immediately along the new route line with no drift, no gather step and no wasted movement between the plant and the acceleration.
rows.fault_trigger: A gather or recovery step between the plant and the first driving step, or the step drifting off the new line - either way the separation the cut created is handed straight back.

rows.ideal_execution_standard: The arms fire back into a violent forward pump the moment the cut is made, mechanically driving the tight end back up to sprinting speed.
rows.fault_trigger: Arms staying tucked or pumping weakly out of the cut, so the upper body contributes nothing to rebuilding speed on the new line.

rows.ideal_execution_standard: The head tracks the target while staying aligned with the new running lane - the tight end finds the ball without letting his body drift off the route line.
rows.fault_trigger: Head turning so far to track the ball that the body follows and drifts off the route line, or losing the target entirely coming out of the break. (Gaze and ball location are not pose-measurable.)

rows.ideal_execution_standard: The hips travel on a strict straight line along the new route path, exiting the cut at a sharp angle rather than curving out of it.
rows.fault_trigger: ROUNDING THE ANGLE - the pelvis trajectory forms a wide curve instead of a sharp linear exit, giving the defender time and space to recover the separation the cut had created.

rows.ideal_execution_standard: The shoulders square up to the new route line and the torso resumes its forward sprinting lean, the body reset into pure acceleration.
rows.fault_trigger: Shoulders staying rotated or the torso staying upright after the cut, so the tight end runs out of the break unbalanced and slow to rebuild speed.

rows.ideal_execution_standard: The lead knee drives high and forward out of the cut, generating maximum instant acceleration back to full speed on the new line.
rows.fault_trigger: Low knee drive out of the break, so the tight end shuffles back up to speed and the window the cut opened closes before the ball arrives.

rows.ideal_execution_standard: The knees drive at full sprint height through the stem, generating the maximum speed that the breakdown will then have to absorb.
rows.fault_trigger: Knee drive dropping off during the stem, slowing the tight end early and removing the vertical threat the stop cut depends on.

rows.ideal_execution_standard: Stride length stays maximal through the vertical stem, holding genuine top speed so the deep threat forces the defender to turn and run.
rows.fault_trigger: TELEGRAPHING - stride shortening or velocity dropping before the breakdown, which warns the defender the tight end is about to stop and lets them sit on the route.

rows.ideal_execution_standard: The arms pump violently through the stem at full sprint amplitude, driving the vertical push and giving no hint the break is coming.
rows.fault_trigger: Arm pump shortening or slowing during the stem, a visual tell that the tight end is about to break down.

rows.ideal_execution_standard: The torso holds an aggressive forward sprint lean through the stem, the posture of a tight end running past the defender rather than one preparing to stop.
rows.fault_trigger: Torso rising toward upright during the stem, an early tell that the tight end is preparing to break down.

rows.ideal_execution_standard: Vision stays locked straight downfield through the stem, maintaining the deep vertical threat that makes the stop work.
rows.fault_trigger: Head turning toward the break during the stem, breaking the vertical threat before the tight end has reached the break point. (Gaze itself is not pose-measurable - orientation only.)

rows.ideal_execution_standard: The hips carry constant high-speed travel down the stem with minimal bounce, selling the vertical route before anything changes.
rows.fault_trigger: Velocity easing off during the stem, so the deep threat is never established and the defender does not have to respect it.

rows.ideal_execution_standard: The hips drop drastically on the breakdown steps, dumping the centre of gravity low so the legs can absorb the speed and the body can anchor.
rows.fault_trigger: STIFF LEG - entering the breakdown with the hips still high, so the deceleration is absorbed through the knees rather than the whole lower body. Slower to stop and hard on the joints.

rows.ideal_execution_standard: Stride shortens rapidly into 2 to 3 chop steps, gathering the feet underneath the body to kill momentum in as little ground as possible.
rows.fault_trigger: Too many chop steps, or a gradual slow-down rather than a sharp gather - the breakdown takes too long and the defender closes the space before the break.

rows.ideal_execution_standard: The forward sprint lean shifts back into a tucked, balanced position with the shoulders inside the knee frame, so the tight end can anchor rather than being carried forward.
rows.fault_trigger: Shoulders staying out over the toes through the breakdown, so momentum carries the chest forward and the tight end cannot stop cleanly or has to take recovery steps.

rows.ideal_execution_standard: Both knees move from maximum sprint drive into deep bilateral flexion, working as shock absorbers to soak up the speed the stem built.
rows.fault_trigger: Knees staying relatively straight through the breakdown, so there is nothing to absorb the momentum - the tight end skids, stumbles, or needs extra steps to stop.

rows.ideal_execution_standard: Vision stays locked downfield through the breakdown steps, holding the deep threat even as the body gathers to stop.
rows.fault_trigger: Head turning during the breakdown rather than at the visual snap, giving the defender an extra beat of warning before the break. (Gaze itself is not pose-measurable - orientation only.)

rows.ideal_execution_standard: The violent sprint pump compacts into a tight position near the chest, quieting the arms so they do not fight the deceleration or unbalance the body.
rows.fault_trigger: Arms still swinging wide through the breakdown, throwing the tight end off balance at exactly the moment he needs to be stable. (Finger and grip detail needs the Hand landmarker.)

rows.ideal_execution_standard: The wide, low stance holds for a beat as forward velocity reaches zero - the tight end is genuinely stopped, not still drifting.
rows.fault_trigger: Still carrying forward velocity through the pause, so the tight end drifts past the break point and the route depth is wrong; or the base narrowing and losing the platform for the plant.

rows.ideal_execution_standard: The hips hold their low position through the pause, staying loaded so the plant can fire without needing to re-sink.
rows.fault_trigger: Hips rising during the pause, unloading the legs - the tight end then has to drop again before he can drive out, and the break is late.

rows.ideal_execution_standard: The shoulders rotate in behind the head turn, shifting the body's equilibrium toward the new break so the plant can redirect immediately.
rows.fault_trigger: Shoulders rotating before or without the head, so the body commits blind and the tight end is late picking up the ball out of the break.

rows.ideal_execution_standard: The hands stay elevated and active in a compact frame through the pause, ready to catch and tight enough not to slow the rotation.
rows.fault_trigger: Hands dropping or going wide during the pause, so the tight end is neither ready for a quick throw nor compact enough to turn fast. (Finger and grip detail needs the Hand landmarker.)

rows.ideal_execution_standard: The deep knee bend is maintained through the pause, keeping the lower body loaded like a spring ready to fire on the plant.
rows.fault_trigger: Knees extending during the pause, so the stored energy leaks away and the drive out has to be generated from scratch.

rows.ideal_execution_standard: The head snaps immediately and fast toward the new route, leading the movement so the eyes find the quarterback before the body has finished turning.
rows.fault_trigger: BLIND TURN - the torso rotates before the eyes do, so the tight end comes out of the break without having found the ball and is late reacting to a throw already in the air. (Gaze itself is not pose-measurable - orientation only.)

rows.ideal_execution_standard: The torso leans securely out over the planting toe, keeping the weight stacked over the anchor so the tight end does not slip backward off the plant.
rows.fault_trigger: Shoulders sitting back behind the plant foot, so the weight is behind the anchor and the tight end slips backward instead of driving out.

rows.ideal_execution_standard: The planting knee flexes deep at contact, building a powerful stopping platform that absorbs the last of the momentum and stores it for the drive out.
rows.fault_trigger: Planting on a straight or shallow-bent leg, which cannot absorb the remaining momentum - the tight end skids through the break or jars to a stop with nothing stored for the exit.

rows.ideal_execution_standard: The outside foot lands with the toe pointing exactly down the new route angle, acting as a steering mechanism rather than just a brake. The toe is pulled up into dorsiflexion so the heel bites the grass first, giving clean, firm contact instead of a slide or a stubbed toe. The step stays compact and lands directly beneath the centre of mass - no over-extending or lunging - which both preserves body control and keeps the defender believing the tight end is still accelerating vertically until the instant the weight drops.
rows.fault_trigger: BLIND PLANT - the toe points straight ahead or wide of the new path, so the foot brakes instead of steering and the tight end slips off the anchor. Toe left down (plantarflexed) rather than pulled up, so the tight end slides through the plant or stubs the toe instead of biting the ground heel-first. Over-extending or lunging the plant step out ahead of the centre of mass, which costs body control and tips the break early by showing the defender the tight end is gathering rather than still running.

rows.ideal_execution_standard: The hips reach their lowest point of the entire cut at the plant - the core locked down against the ground, giving the anchor maximum stability.
rows.fault_trigger: Hips already rising at the plant rather than bottoming out, so the anchor is weak and the tight end gets carried past the break point.

rows.ideal_execution_standard: The head snap lands on exactly the same instant as the cleat hits the ground - eyes and anchor arriving together, so the tight end is looking at the quarterback the moment he is able to catch.
rows.fault_trigger: Head snap arriving before or after cleat impact rather than with it - either the tight end tips the break early, or he is still turning when the ball is already on its way.

rows.ideal_execution_standard: The arms fire back into a violent punch-like pump the instant the drive out begins, mechanically restoring sprint momentum from a standing stop.
rows.fault_trigger: Arms staying compact or pumping weakly out of the break, so the upper body adds nothing to rebuilding speed from a dead stop - where it matters most.

rows.ideal_execution_standard: The lead knee drives immediately up and forward out of the plant, converting the stored energy into instant acceleration on the new line.
rows.fault_trigger: Low knee drive out of the break, so the tight end shuffles back up to speed and the throwing window closes before he can separate.

rows.ideal_execution_standard: The shoulders square up to the new path and the torso resumes its forward sprint lean, the body reset from stopping posture into pure acceleration.
rows.fault_trigger: Shoulders staying rotated or the torso staying upright and tucked after the break, so the tight end runs out slow and unbalanced on the new line.

rows.ideal_execution_standard: The hips rotate rapidly to sit parallel with the new exit trajectory, locking the tight end onto a sharp straight line out of the break.
rows.fault_trigger: ROUNDING - the exit trajectory curves rather than forming a sharp line, so the defender recovers the ground the stop had won. Usually caused by the hips rotating too slowly out of the plant.

rows.ideal_execution_standard: The tight end pushes explosively off the instep of the plant foot into a low, linear first step - the anchor converts straight into acceleration with nothing wasted.
rows.fault_trigger: A gather step between the plant and the drive out, or a high, short first step - either way the stored energy is wasted and the defender recovers the separation the stop created.

rows.ideal_execution_standard: Vision stays locked on the quarterback through the drive out, tracking the throw while the body holds its line on the new trajectory.
rows.fault_trigger: Losing the quarterback coming out of the break, or turning the head so far that the body follows and the exit line curves off the route. (Gaze and ball location are not pose-measurable.)

rows.ideal_execution_standard: Explode off the line and sprint at full vertical velocity for 12-15 yards, forcing the defender to turn their hips into a deep, desperate retreat. At break depth, violently sink the hips and chop the cleats rapidly into the turf - the sudden lowering of the centre of gravity is the braking system that halts forward momentum.
rows.fault_trigger: STIFF-LEGGED BRAKING - trying to stop without sinking the hips. The tight end stumbles forward, takes too many recovery steps, and puts dangerous stress on the knees. (Absolute depth needs a scale reference and the declared route.)

rows.ideal_execution_standard: The millisecond forward momentum halts, snap the head and eyes back around over the inside shoulder to face the quarterback first. Turning the vision inside opens the upper torso and picks up the ball's trajectory before the lower body has finished its pivot.
rows.fault_trigger: Head coming round late or after the body has pivoted, so the tight end finishes the break without having found the quarterback - and a ball already in the air arrives before he is looking for it. (Gaze and ball location are not pose-measurable.)

rows.ideal_execution_standard: As the eyes find the quarterback, drive the outside cutting foot down into a tight, compact step directly under the hips. The toe is pulled up sharply into dorsiflexion right before contact, striking heel and midfoot first to lock the brakes instantly. Pivot and direct the toe at a 45-degree angle back down the stem toward the sideline.
rows.fault_trigger: THE LUNGING TOE PLANT - reaching too far forward with the planting step and letting the toe point downward before contact. This strips core stability, causes a slide, and tips off the defender early because the running stride visibly changes before the cut.

rows.ideal_execution_standard: Drive powerfully off the inside instep of the directing foot and work back downhill toward the ball, shortening the distance of the throw, squaring the shoulders to the quarterback to shield the ball, and securing the catch with the hands extended away from the frame.
rows.fault_trigger: WAITING ON THE BALL - standing still after making the cut. The tight end must actively run back downhill toward the ball to stop a trailing defender undercutting the route for an interception. (Ball position and defender leverage are not pose-measurable.)

rows.ideal_execution_standard: Drive off the line at full velocity for 10-12 yards (12-15 on the deeper variation) with pads leaning forward and long natural strides, pushing the defender into a deep vertical retreat. One step before the break, subtly drop the hips an inch to gather balance and prepare the core for high-speed redirection - without chopping or stutter-stepping.
rows.fault_trigger: FADING EARLY - unconsciously drifting outward toward the sideline before the break depth, alerting the defender to clamp down on the corner. (Absolute depth needs a scale reference and the called depth.)

rows.ideal_execution_standard: At break depth, snap the head and eyes sharply toward the corner pylon first. The rapid visual rotation opens the upper torso and shifts equilibrium toward the outside before the lower body begins to pivot.
rows.fault_trigger: Head turning with the plant or after it rather than leading it, so the torso never pre-rotates and the break is slower and squarer than it should be. (Gaze itself is not pose-measurable - orientation only.)

rows.ideal_execution_standard: As the eyes lock onto the pylon, drive the INSIDE foot down into a tight, compact step directly under the centre of mass. The toe is pulled up sharply into dorsiflexion right before contact, striking with a rigid foot. Instantly point the toe down a 45-degree track toward the corner, masking the break until the last possible instant.
rows.fault_trigger: THE LUNGING SLIDE - lunging too far forward with a loose, downward-pointing toe. The over-extension lacks the rigidity to anchor a 45-degree turn, so the shoe slides over the grass and the defender closes the gap.

rows.ideal_execution_standard: Push violently off the inside instep of the directing foot, flip the hips wide open, and punch the outside arm across the body to accelerate along a strict 45-degree line toward the corner.
rows.fault_trigger: FLATTENING THE ANGLE - letting the route angle flat toward the sideline rather than holding a strict 45 degrees toward the corner pylon, which shortens the route and lets the defender close.

rows.ideal_execution_standard: Explode vertically off the line for 2 to 3 hard steps, driving the pads forward to threaten the defender's leverage and make them respect the go route. Then prepare to redirect sideways by subtly sinking the hips, keeping the feet moving at full speed with no choppy or gathering steps.
rows.fault_trigger: FADING EARLY - drifting inward toward the middle of the field right off the snap. This tells the defender exactly where the tight end is going and lets them squeeze him into the linebacker level. (Absolute depth needs a scale reference.)

rows.ideal_execution_standard: At break depth, snap the head and eyes sharply across the formation first. The visual focus locks onto the open grass underneath the linebackers, which naturally uncoils the neck and shoulders into the cross lane.
rows.fault_trigger: Head turning with the plant or after it rather than leading it, so the shoulders never uncoil into the lane and the tight end crosses without having seen the linebacker level. (Gaze and defender positions are not pose-measurable.)

rows.ideal_execution_standard: The instant the eyes find the cross lane, drive the outside foot down into a sharp, compact step positioned firmly beneath the body weight. The toe is pulled up before the foot strikes to ground cleanly. Instantly point the toe and direct the final step down a flat 90-degree track across the field, masking the horizontal break until the last possible instant.
rows.fault_trigger: THE DOWNFIELD TOE PLANT - planting with the toe still pointing toward the end zone. Failing to direct the foot at 90 degrees causes the tight end to drift downfield, running straight into the waiting linebackers.

rows.ideal_execution_standard: Push violently off the inside instep of the directing foot, sprint flat along the line across the formation, snap the eyes back over the inside shoulder to look for the ball, and secure the catch while bracing to turn upfield.
rows.fault_trigger: BUBBLING THE ROUTE - letting the route angle backward toward the line of scrimmage or bubble downfield. The line must stay flat and parallel to the line of scrimmage to maximise the open void. (Ball location needs ball tracking.)

rows.ideal_execution_standard: Explode off the ball and sprint at full vertical velocity to roughly 12 yards, holding a low pad level and natural full strides to drive the defender into a deep backpedal. At break depth, violently sink the hips and chop the cleats rapidly into the turf - the sudden lowering of the centre of gravity is the braking system that halts the momentum the longer stem has built.
rows.fault_trigger: TELEGRAPHING THE STOP - slowing down or rising out of the low pad level a couple of yards before the break point, which lets the defender instantly close the cushion. STIFF-LEGGED BRAKING - trying to stop without sinking the hips, causing a stumble, extra recovery steps, and dangerous stress on the knees.

rows.ideal_execution_standard: The millisecond forward momentum halts, snap the head and eyes back around over the inside shoulder to face the quarterback first. Turning the vision inside opens the upper torso and picks up the ball's trajectory before the lower body has finished its pivot.
rows.fault_trigger: Head coming round late or after the body has pivoted, so the tight end finishes the break without having found the quarterback - and a ball already in the air arrives before he is looking for it. (Gaze and ball location are not pose-measurable.)

rows.ideal_execution_standard: As the eyes find the quarterback, drive the cutting foot down into a tight, compact step directly under the hips. The toe is pulled up sharply into dorsiflexion right before contact, striking with a rigid foot to lock the brakes instantly. Pivot and direct the toe back down the stem toward the line of scrimmage, holding the illusion of a forward sprint until the exact moment of the cut.
rows.fault_trigger: THE LUNGING TOE PLANT - reaching too far forward with the planting step and letting the toe point downward before contact. This strips core stability, causes a slide, and tips off the defender early because the running stride visibly changes before the cut.

rows.ideal_execution_standard: Drive powerfully off the inside instep of the directing foot, open the chest completely to the quarterback, work back downhill toward the ball to shorten the distance of the throw, and secure the catch with the hands extended away from the frame.
rows.fault_trigger: WAITING ON THE BALL - standing still after making the cut. The tight end must actively run back downhill toward the ball to stop a trailing defender undercutting the route for an interception. (Ball position and defender leverage are not pose-measurable.)

rows.ideal_execution_standard: Run an ultra-aggressive vertical stem for 12-15 yards, pushing directly at the defender's midsection to freeze their leverage and force a deep backpedal respecting the post or go. At break depth, violently drop the weight into the hips and chop the cleats heavily through a 3-step breakdown to absorb the extra momentum the longer stem has built.
rows.fault_trigger: BANANA STEMMING - curving the path inward before making the actual break. A rounded line lets an inside-shade defender stay in front of the tight end the whole way. (Absolute depth needs a scale reference and the declared route.)

rows.ideal_execution_standard: At the absolute peak of the breakdown, snap the head and eyes around to face the quarterback first. The visual snap opens the torso and clears vision to read the inside linebackers before the body commits.
rows.fault_trigger: Head turning with or after the plant rather than leading it, so the tight end breaks into the middle without having cleared his vision for crashing inside defenders. (Gaze and defender positions are not pose-measurable.)

rows.ideal_execution_standard: The instant the eyes locate the inside lane, drive the outside cutting foot down into a compact step tightly aligned within the frame. The toe is pulled upward into dorsiflexion right before contact to establish a firm ankle lock. The cleat slams down directly beneath the hips, instantly pointing the toe at a sharp 90-degree angle toward the middle of the field.
rows.fault_trigger: OVERSTRIDING THE BREAK - reaching too far inside with a long, diving step. This elongates the body frame, tells the defender exactly when the break is coming, and locks up the hips so the tight end cannot accelerate smoothly out of the cut. Also: THE FLOPPY-FOOT SLIDE - planting with a loose, downward-pointing toe out in front of the chest, lacking the rigidity to anchor a 90-degree turn, so the shoe slides over the grass.

rows.ideal_execution_standard: Drive powerfully off the inside instep of the directing foot, snap the hips wide open, and punch the outside arm across the body to accelerate flat across the field, holding a low, aggressive acceleration posture.
rows.fault_trigger: RUNNING FLAT / BANANING - letting the route drift downfield toward the defensive backfield instead of holding a flat, razor-sharp 90-degree line across the middle.

rows.ideal_execution_standard: At break depth, snap the head and eyes sharply toward the sideline first. The visual focus locks onto the boundary line, which naturally uncoils the neck and shoulders into the flat lane.
rows.fault_trigger: Head turning with the plant or after it rather than leading it, so the shoulders never uncoil into the lane and the break is slower than a quick-game route can afford. (Gaze itself is not pose-measurable - orientation only.)

rows.ideal_execution_standard: The instant the eyes find the sideline, drive the INSIDE foot down into a sharp, compact step positioned firmly beneath the body weight. The toe is pulled up into dorsiflexion before the foot strikes to ground cleanly. rows.ideal_execution_standard: Push violently off the inside instep of the directing foot, sprint flat along the line toward the boundary, snap the eyes back over the inside shoulder to look for the ball, and secure the catch while bracing to turn upfield.
rows.fault_trigger: DRIFTING DOWNHILL - allowing the route to angle backward toward the line of scrimmage. The line must stay flat and parallel to the line of scrimmage to maximise the open void. (Ball location needs ball tracking.)

rows.ideal_execution_standard: Explode off the ball with a violent, low pad-level release to clear the press defender's hands and establish the vertical track, then transition from acceleration into full top-speed sprint posture - stride lengths opening to maximum expansion with the chin tucked.
rows.fault_trigger: Standing up out of the release rather than driving low, or strides failing to expand into top-end sprint mechanics - either way the tight end never reaches the speed the route depends on.

rows.ideal_execution_standard: Running neck-and-neck with the defender, use a high-speed hand swipe or arm bar to clear their trailing reach, working to stack the body directly in front of their path and strip away their recovery angle - while the head stays locked downfield.
rows.fault_trigger: LOOKING BACK EARLY - turning the head to look for the ball while it is still in the air and outside the catch radius. Looking back early kills top-end speed and tells the defender to play the hands. (Defender position and stack are not pose-measurable.)

rows.ideal_execution_standard: The running stride stays completely natural and uninterrupted, steps landing compact and directly beneath the centre of mass without overstriding. The toes pull up into sharp dorsiflexion on every stride to hold a rigid, explosive ankle lock against the turf while the eyes track the ball over the shoulder.
rows.fault_trigger: OVERSTRIDING / FLOPPY FOOTWORK - reaching too far forward to try to run faster, or running with a loose, downward-pointing toe. This strips core stability, caps top-end speed, and costs balance down the sideline.

rows.ideal_execution_standard: Keep the hands down and running until the absolute last moment so the defender is not tipped off to the ball's arrival, then shoot the arms out late, secure the catch away from the frame, and protect the ball.
rows.fault_trigger: EARLY HANDS - running with the hands extended upward for several yards waiting for the ball. This is a clear signal to the defender, letting them play the arms and break up the pass. (Ball arrival timing needs ball tracking.)

Two steps before break depth, violently sink the hips and chop the cleats to control speed - without standing up or slowing the arm pump.
rows.fault_trigger: THE DEAD GIVEAWAY - slowing the arm pump or raising the chest before reaching break depth, alerting the defender to clamp down on the out route. (Absolute depth needs a scale reference and the declared route.)

rows.ideal_execution_standard: At the exact peak of deceleration, snap the head and eyes sharply toward the sideline first. The visual turn shifts equilibrium and opens the upper torso toward the boundary before the feet leave the turf.
rows.fault_trigger: Head turning at the same time as the plant or after it, so the body commits before the eyes have opened the boundary - the torso does not pre-rotate and the break is slower. (Gaze itself is not pose-measurable - orientation only.)

The toe is pulled up sharply into dorsiflexion right before contact, striking with a rigid foot to lock the brakes. Instantly pivot and point the toe down a flat 90-degree track toward the sideline, masking the break until the last possible instant.

One step before the break, drop the weight subtly into the hips and prepare to transfer laterally - without any choppy or gathering steps.
